div.head: II Cn 81
div.ab: And drincelean ⁊ hlafordes rihtgifu stande æfre unawend.
And drincelean ⁊ hlafordes rihtgyfu stande æfre unawend.
[81] Et drinceléan (id est retributio potus) et domini rectum donum semper stet inconuulsum.
⁊ dryncelean ⁊ hlafordes rihtgyfu stande æfre unawended.
And drincelean and hlafordes rihtgifu stande æfre unawend.
Und ‘Trinklohn’ [Vertragsabschluss oder Nordisch Landgabe für Bewirthung] und des Herrn gesetzliche Schenkung bestehe immer unverrückt.
And let ‘drink-reward’ [conclusion of a contract, or in Norse usage a grant of land for hospitality] and the lord's lawful gift always stand unaltered.
And there shall never be any interference with bargains successfully concluded or with the legal gifts made by a lord.
And drincelean and the lord’s legal gift are to remain ever unperverted.
And let the negotiated contract and the lord’s legal gift always remain unaltered.
div.note: Liebermann compares III Atr 3.; AP: corrected against Whitelock p. 474, October 2026 (was “And drincelean and the lord’s legal gift are to remain ever unperverted.”, now “And drincelean and the lord’s legal gift are to remain ever unperverted. (expanded letters in italics: drincelean)”)
negotiated contract: Old English drincelean literally refers to the drink that seals a negotiation, signaling the agreement of all parties and the legitimacy of the transaction.

S. Gl Vertrag 4; Grundbesitz 4. 6—c. Jedenfalls zu verwerfen ist die Beziehung zu scotale (Abgabe für Bier oder statt Bierabkauf vom Hintersassen an Herrn oder Vogt) und Verbindung mit bargilden, angeblich ‘Bierzinsern’.—Die Nordische Erklärung gaben zuerst Steenstrup Danelag 187; Maurer Gesetzspr. in Dän. in SB Münch. Ak. 1887, 396

See Gl Vertrag 4; Grundbesitz 4. 6—c. The connexion with scotale (a payment for beer, or in lieu of buying beer, from the dependent tenant to the lord or reeve) and the link with bargilden, supposedly ‘beer-rent payers’, are in any case to be rejected.—The Norse explanation was first given by Steenstrup Danelag 187; Maurer Gesetzspr. in Dän. in SB Münch. Ak. 1887, 396

The exact significance of the word dryncelean is uncertain. It is regarded by Steenstrup (Danelag, p. 187) as equivalent to the Scandinavian drekkulaun, i.e. land bestowed as a gift by the king in return for hospitality (see also Amira, Nordgerm. Oblig. ii. p. 619). It seems possible, however, that a gift of ‘drink-money’ may have marked the successful conclusion of a bargain, see Anglia, 33 (1910), p. 134; Gierke, Schuld und Haftung, p. 368 f. In the twelfth century 1 penny had to be paid as drink money (beverache) by a buyer of land at Whitby, see Bateson, Borough Customs, ii. p. 81.

note.label: drincelean
note.seg: A word of uncertain meaning, cf. No. 52, p. 476. It may be “granting of drink” and refer to the custom of drinking to mark the conclusion of a compact, or it may, like its Old Norse equivalent, drekkulaun, refer to a gift (in Scandinavia, of land from the king) made in return for hospitality, thus meaning “reward for drink”.
